---
title: "From Text to Numbers"
subtitle: "What has to happen before a language model can learn from text"
---

*Prerequisites: none. This page comes before `learn/neural-networks.qmd`
in the course sequence, but neither page assumes the other.*

## 1. The problem being solved

A neural network computes with numbers. Each of its units takes a list of
numbers in, forms a weighted sum, applies a fixed nonlinear function, and
passes the result on; `learn/neural-networks.qmd` works one such unit
through in full. Text is not a list of numbers. A sentence is a string of
characters, and there is no arithmetic to do on the letter "b". So before
any learning can happen, every piece of training text, and later every
prompt, has to be turned into numbers that a network can operate on.

The conversion has to satisfy two requirements at once. It must be
mechanical and consistent, so that the same text always becomes the same
numbers, during training and afterwards. And it must produce numbers the
network can *improve*: numbers that training is allowed to adjust so that
they become useful for prediction, rather than fixed codes chosen by a
person. Those two requirements are met by three steps, taken in order:

1. split the text into units drawn from a fixed inventory ([**tokens**](../glossary.qmd#token));
2. replace each unit by its index in that inventory ([**token IDs**](../glossary.qmd#token-id));
3. replace each index by a list of adjustable numbers looked up from a
   table ([**embedding vectors**](../glossary.qmd#embedding)).

The rest of this page follows one short sentence through those three
steps, then explains what the network is asked to do with the result and
where training takes over.

### Before any of this: assembling the training text

The sentence in §2 stands in for an enormous body of text, and that body
does not arrive ready-made. Before tokenization there is a data
pipeline: source material is gathered from web pages, code, books, and
other permitted sources; the main text is extracted from its raw form;
documents are filtered by language and by quality rules; duplicates are
removed; and only the surviving text is handed to the tokenizer. In
short, raw source material → curated corpus → tokenizer → tokens. One
open, documented example of such a pipeline is Hugging Face's FineWeb
dataset, built from Common Crawl web snapshots by URL filtering, text
extraction, language filtering, quality filtering, and deduplication.
[S-78] It is one open example of the kind of work involved, not a
description of any particular model's corpus: complete training corpora
for closed models are often not publicly disclosed, the level of
disclosure varies across models and providers, corpora differ between
models, and "trained on the internet" is shorthand for a curated
selection, not a literal description.

## 2. A small example

The running example is the sentence

> "The bridge was closed."

By the end of §6 it will have become an array of numbers with one row per
token, and by the end of §7 it will also have supplied the answers the
network is trained to predict.

## 3. Splitting text into tokens

The first step cuts the text into pieces. The pieces come from a fixed
inventory, called the [**vocabulary**](../glossary.qmd#vocabulary), that is decided once, before
training, and then used unchanged for all text the model ever sees. The
program that does the cutting is the [**tokenizer**](../glossary.qmd#tokenizer). The pieces it produces
are tokens, and they are often whole words, but not always: a common word
may be one token, a rare or long word may be split into several, and in
many commonly used tokenizers spaces and punctuation influence the split.

For the running example, an illustrative tokenizer might produce five
tokens:

| Position | Token |
|---|---|
| 1 | `The` |
| 2 | ` bridge` |
| 3 | ` was` |
| 4 | ` closed` |
| 5 | `.` |

Two details of this split are worth noticing, because they are typical of
many commonly used tokenizers. The space before a word is part of the
token (` bridge` with a leading space is a different token from `bridge`
without one), and the full stop is its own token. In the tokenizer used by
GPT-2, for example, spaces were deliberately allowed to merge with the
word that follows them, while punctuation was kept from merging with
words. [S-28]

The split above is **illustrative**. It is not the exact tokenization any
particular current model would produce; different model families use
different tokenizers, and the same sentence can be cut differently by
each. What is not illustrative is the shape of the outcome: a fixed
vocabulary, typically tens of thousands of entries (GPT-2's had 50,257),
and a sequence of tokens drawn from it. [S-28] How a vocabulary like that
is built, and why models use word fragments rather than characters or
whole words, is the subject of `learn/tokens-context.qmd`.

## 4. From tokens to token IDs

Each entry in the vocabulary has a position in it, an integer from 0 up to
the vocabulary size minus one. Replacing each token by that integer gives
the **token ID**. For the running example, with made-up numbers:

| Position | Token | Token ID (illustrative) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `The` | 1032 |
| 2 | ` bridge` | 2471 |
| 3 | ` was` | 88 |
| 4 | ` closed` | 5109 |
| 5 | `.` | 12 |

A token ID is an address, and nothing more. The number 5109 is not
"larger" than 88 in any sense that matters to the model: ` closed` is not
more of anything than ` was`, and IDs that are close together are not
similar tokens. The network never adds, compares, or multiplies token
IDs. It uses each one only to look up a row in a table, which is the next
step. A different tokenizer would assign entirely different numbers to the
same pieces, and the model built on it would work just as well.

## 5. From token IDs to embedding vectors

The network needs each token to arrive as a list of numbers it can do
arithmetic on. That list is a **vector**: an ordered list of $d$ real
numbers, written for example as $(0.21, -0.60, 0.05)$ when $d = 3$. Every
token gets a vector of the same length $d$.

The vectors live in a table with one row per vocabulary entry and $d$
columns, called the **embedding table** and written $E$. Converting a
token ID to its vector is a row lookup:

$$
\mathbf{e}_t = E_{\text{id}_t}
$$

Here $\text{id}_t$ is the token ID at position $t$, $E_{\text{id}_t}$ is
the row of the table with that index, and $\mathbf{e}_t$ is the resulting
vector, the **embedding** of the token at position $t$. For the running
example, with $d = 3$ and made-up entries:

| Position | Token | Token ID | Embedding vector (illustrative, $d = 3$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `The` | 1032 | $(0.21, -0.60, 0.05)$ |
| 2 | ` bridge` | 2471 | $(-0.33, 0.14, 0.92)$ |
| 3 | ` was` | 88 | $(0.08, 0.47, -0.21)$ |
| 4 | ` closed` | 5109 | $(0.55, -0.12, 0.30)$ |
| 5 | `.` | 12 | $(-0.70, 0.02, -0.15)$ |

Where do these numbers come from? Not from a dictionary. Nothing in the
row for ` bridge` encodes "a structure carrying a road over a river". The
entries of $E$ are [**parameters**](../glossary.qmd#parameter) of the model, in exactly the sense that
the weights and biases of a unit are parameters: they start as arbitrary
values and are adjusted by training, together with every other parameter,
so that the network's predictions improve. The idea of learning a vector
for each word jointly with the rest of a language model goes back to an
early neural language model, in which the table of word vectors was
explicitly a matrix of free parameters with one row per vocabulary entry;
the transformer uses a learned embedding table in the same way. [S-29]
[S-30] Whatever usefulness a row of $E$ ends up having is a result of
training, not something written into it in advance.

The length $d$ is a design choice. In that early model the vectors had
30 to 100 entries. [S-29] Real vectors have far too many entries to print;
the $d = 3$ table above is only to show the shape.

## 6. What the model receives

After the three steps, the sentence has become five vectors of length
$d$, one per token, in order. Stacked, they form an array with $n = 5$
rows and $d$ columns. That array, not the sentence, is what enters the
network.

One thing is missing from that array. The token vectors alone carry no
information about order: the row looked up for ` bridge` is the same
whether the token is first or fifth, and nothing in the stack of rows
says which came before which. A transformer therefore needs an explicit
mechanism that lets it distinguish positions. The original Transformer
added a positional encoding to each input embedding; other transformer
architectures provide position information in other ways. [S-30] The
mechanics of that step, and of what the layers then do, belong to later
pages.

So the answer to "what does the model actually receive instead of a
sentence?" is: a sequence of $n$ vectors, one per token, each looked up
from a learned table by the token's ID, together with a mechanism that
lets the architecture tell the positions apart. None of it is a letter, a
word, or a meaning.

## 7. What the model is asked to predict

Autoregressive language models, the kind this course is about, are
pretrained by predicting the next token from the tokens that came before
it. The running example supplies its own answers. Reading the five tokens
left to right, the input at each position and the target the model
should predict are:

| Position | Input so far | Target (next token) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `The` | ` bridge` |
| 2 | `The` ` bridge` | ` was` |
| 3 | `The` ` bridge` ` was` | ` closed` |
| 4 | `The` ` bridge` ` was` ` closed` | `.` |

The targets are the text shifted by one position. No person had to label
anything: each position for which a following token is available supplies
a prediction target automatically. At each position the network's output is not
a single guess but a probability distribution over the entire
vocabulary, and the target is a token ID, an index into that same
vocabulary. [S-05] How raw output scores become that distribution is the
subject of `learn/softmax-sampling.qmd`; some models even reuse the
embedding table $E$ for the final step that produces one score per
vocabulary entry. [S-30]

## 8. Where training takes over

Two of the three steps above are fixed for the life of the model: the
tokenizer's splitting rule and the mapping from vocabulary entries to
IDs are decided once and never learned. The third is different. The
embedding lookup itself is part of every forward computation, and the
entries of the table it reads from are parameters, updated during
training. Training is what happens next, and the ingredients are the
ones `learn/neural-networks.qmd` works through on a single unit: a
forward pass produces the predicted
distribution at each position; a loss measures how much probability was
assigned to the actual next token; backpropagation computes how the loss
would change with a small change in each parameter; and an optimizer
adjusts the parameters, the rows of the embedding table among them, which
is why the vectors in §5 end up useful even though they started
arbitrary. Doing this over an enormous body of text
is pretraining, covered in a later lesson. This page stops at the
handoff: the network now has numbers to compute with and a target to
compare against.

## 9. A common misconception

**"The model looks each word up in a dictionary."** The embedding step is
a lookup, so the confusion is understandable, but what is looked up is a
row of adjustable numbers, not a definition. The row has no content
before training and acquires whatever structure it has only because
adjusting it helped the network predict next tokens. A related confusion
treats token IDs as measurements: they are not. A token ID is an index
into a table, and two IDs being numerically close says nothing about the
tokens.

## 10. Check your understanding

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>The model is given the sentence "The bridge was closed." What
does it actually receive?</summary>
A sequence of vectors, one per token: the sentence is split into tokens
by the tokenizer, each token is replaced by its ID, each ID selects a row
of the learned embedding table, and the architecture supplies a way to
tell the positions apart. The network operates on that array of numbers,
never on the characters (§6).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>Token ` closed` has ID 5109 and token ` was` has ID 88 in the
illustrative table. Does the larger number mean anything?</summary>
No. A token ID is an index into the vocabulary and is used only to look
up a row of the embedding table. The model never does arithmetic on IDs,
and numerically close IDs are not similar tokens (§4).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>Where do the numbers in an embedding vector come from?</summary>
They are parameters of the model. They start as arbitrary values and are
adjusted during training, together with all the other parameters, so that
the network's next-token predictions improve. They are not dictionary
definitions stored as numbers (§5).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>Who supplies the correct answers the model is trained
against?</summary>
The text itself. At each position that has a following token, the target
is simply that next token, so the training text supplies its own targets
without any human labeling (§7).
</details>
:::

## 11. Continue learning

- **`learn/tokens-context.qmd`** (this course). The deep dive on how a
  vocabulary is built, why tokens are word fragments, what the embedding
  table does and does not encode, and what the finite context window
  implies in practice.

- **Bengio, Ducharme, Vincent, and Jauvin, *A Neural Probabilistic
  Language Model*** (paper, Journal of Machine Learning Research 3,
  2003; Sections 1 and 2 are enough for this page's point). Technical
  level. The clearest early statement of the idea in §5: learn a vector
  for each word jointly with the model that predicts the next word.
  Limitation: the network it describes is not a transformer, and the
  vocabulary is words, not subword tokens.
  <https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume3/bengio03a/bengio03a.pdf>

- **Andrej Karpathy, *Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT*** (video, 3.5
  hours, including a walkthrough of tokenization). Introductory level,
  plain language. Especially good for seeing real text being split into
  tokens and assigned IDs by an actual tokenizer. Limitation: the
  specific tokenizer and numbers shown are one model's, and the location
  of the tokenization segment within the video has not been verified for
  this course, so no timestamp is given.
  <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI>

See `resources.qmd` for the complete list of sources used across this
course, with full source-map entries.
